summary:
Storm Sheild is a web app that helps astronauts assess their own health and respond to emergencies when Earth can’t answer in time, with a solar-storm early warning as its signature feature. A clickable Health Twin gathers blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood, judges each astronaut against their own baseline, and shows Normal, Watch or Act. Storm Alert turns NASA and NOAA space-weather data into three crew levels with clear actions, then prompts a body check. When someone falls ill, Care Mode guides the crew step by step from cited public sources, Retrace handles the unexpected, Crew Alert calls the rest of the crew, and a structured handoff records everything for the doctor. It matters because Mars-class missions face communication delays of tens of minutes, so crews may have to act first. A human performs every action, guidance is pending medical review, and all crew vitals are simulated and labelled.
Whether the storm is in space or inside an astronaut’s body, Storm Shield shows the crew what to do next, so no one is left in the dark.
details:
What it does. Storm Sheild is a web app for astronauts on Moon and Mars missions, where communication delays can leave the crew to act first. It has three connected parts. Storm Alert turns space-weather data into three crew levels (Watch, Warning, Shelter now) with clear actions, onset, intensity and a “Why this alert?” explanation, then prompts a body check. The Health Twin is a clickable body for each astronaut. It gathers blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood, judges each reading against that person’s own baseline first and general ranges second, and shows Normal, Watch or Act with reasons. Care Mode guides the crew step by step through two scenarios (a cardiovascular scare and illness after a solar storm), using steps from cited public sources, recheck timers and a handoff log. Retrace is a fill-in form for events outside those scenarios. It rebuilds the timeline, flags red signs and suggests the lowest-risk next steps, always marked low confidence. Crew Alert and Self-Support alert the other crew and keep the patient supported until help arrives.

Benefits and intended impact. Crews always see one safe next action, the rest of the crew is alerted quickly, and ground doctors get a structured, time-stamped record. The same approach could support remote clinics on Earth.

How it was built. React and Vite, with all rules in a separate engine covered by 44 automated tests. Content (scenarios, thresholds, sources) lives in JSON files, so it can be reviewed without touching code. It runs in the browser with no backend and works offline. Hosted on Vercel, code on GitHub under the MIT license. Data: NASA CCMC DONKI and NOAA SWPC space-weather information, NASA Human Research Program and Artemis I radiation measurements, and CDC and NIH MedlinePlus first-aid and radiation-illness guidance.
AI tools: Claude, Google Antigravity, Gemini

What is creative. The storm-to-body chain links a real space-weather event to each astronaut’s own health picture. Retrace handles the unexpected, and a simulated wearable-style feed shows how readings could trigger alerts. Every number carries a label (real, published, anchored or simulated) and every step shows its source and review status.

What we considered. A human performs every action; the software recommends and records. All clinical guidance is pending medical review, and crew vitals are simulated because real astronaut data is private. We paraphrased and credited sources, recorded their licenses, and avoided claiming diagnosis or clinical validation.

• Storm Sheild is the project. • Storm Alert covers the storm outside. • Health Copilot covers the storm inside (Health Twin, Care Mode, Retrace).

Storm Shield protects astronauts from two kinds of storms: the solar storm outside the ship and the health storm inside the body. It warns of the first, watches for the second, and at every moment shows the crew what to do next.
